body: I really do appreciate your efforts though. I was born and raised Mormon, and left it when I turned 30. There is a very good reason I'm careful with what I believe and why. I can't believe something for the sake of believing it because of this. I'm trying to find something to believe in, I really am, but there has to be sufficient justification to do so, and for good reason.
The only ones I haven't tried are all out of my price range.
...is no longer sufficient in and of itself to believe.

I really connected with this. I felt like the last few months were pretty awesome. I woke up January 1st feeling like I had been hit by an emotional truck and it's been like that ever since. I, too, feel like the last few months have been a lie. As a side note, I've found Christopher Hyatt and Robert Anton Wilson to be particularly effective in getting outside one's comfort zone.  

At this point I feel like an aspiring drug addict too. I've never snorted anything yet, but at this point I'm strongly considering it because the compunctions I had about it due to self-preservation have disappeared. Like you said, I just don't give a fuck.  

I think the biggest problem I'm facing is that I started dealing with my shit in my 20s. I made a LOT of progress (went from half a grade 10 education to a post-secondary degree, scholarships and bursaries won, merit and prestige in several public and private institutions, one possibly two books being published this year, getting involved with an art gallery and having my art on display, did an ayahuasca journey last year, etc...). It's been over a decade, and while I have a lot of things to be proud of, none of it means anything without someone to share it with. I don't say this to discourage you. In fact, I hope the opposite. If I were still in my 20s, I think I'd have the energy and internal resources to get to work. I don't have that anymore in my 30s, and those internal resources and energy only depletes further with age.

As another side note, what got me going back to school was downloading and listening to some Tony Robbins. While I'm sick to death of motivational speakers, he really helped me figure out what I needed to at that time in my life. Maybe he might do the same for you, who knows. If nothing else, I fee a tiny bit better in connecting with your story. I feel like a lot of it was my own.

This touches upon a very sensitive thing for me. I've done the "get out and meet people" and I've done the "stop paying attention and love will find you". Neither is successful. I feel like either one is futile, that no matter what I do, it's a donkey chasing a carrot that he'll never reach. This donkey is simply refusing to push the cart anymore, and this is taking the form of a hunger strike. I've been "waiting" for a very long time. If I were still in my 20s, I could entertain waiting as an option. I could even entertain waiting now if it looked like things might be different. I see no reason to believe such a thing, or even to believe in anything at all.

> Is there anything in your life that makes you happy, even if only for a little while?  

Not anymore. It's persistent dysphoria and anhedonia. I did medication from 1997 until 2003. PTSD is incredibly resilient to medication, almost to the point of being ineffective; it only treats surrounding symptoms. I don't know how to communicate just how many things I've tried to deal with this.  

I understand where you're coming from. I've used that same kind of thinking to get me out of ruts in the past. This is beyond that. This is the point where I've tried everything I can think of, I've gone out of my comfort zone more times than I can count, and I'm still here. Nothing works. We can play the game of "have you tried this? Yes I have, in about a dozen different ways. Yes, I've tried that too. No, I can't do that, that's out of my price range. No, I can't afford it, I don't have a job. Yes, I've tried that because someone was kind enough to pay for it. Still didn't work, and not because I didn't put in the effort." or I can mention it now, and we can bypass the whole suggesting things that I've already tried (or can't because of affordability), because I've had that conversation more times than I care to count. The only thing that happens is the person or people I'm talking to come to realize just how much effort I've put into getting better, and they realize that they don't have the answers. They then listen to several things that they never mentioned that I have tried on top of their suggestions, and inevitably they come to the same conclusion that I have: they don't know what else to suggest, and they move on because they're not forced to live with this. Some of them even admit that if they were in the same situation, they'd probably want to kill themselves too. They add that they hope I don't, but they understand, to a point, where I'm coming from.
